text: Clustering groups rows. Dimensionality reduction does something complementary — it shrinks columns. Real datasets often carry dozens or hundreds of features, many saying nearly the same thing. Principal component analysis finds a smaller set of new features, called components, that capture as much of the original variation as possible.

Imagine two features that move together, like a customer's app sessions and email opens — instead of tracking both, you could draw one line through the cloud of points and describe each customer by their position along it. PCA does this in general — the first component is the direction the data varies the most, the second is the most remaining variation at a right angle to the first, and so on.

Generating 400 seeded customers with six features really driven by just two hidden factors — engagement and value: visits and app sessions correlate at 0.9, annual spend and basket size correlate at 0.95, but visits and annual spend barely correlate at negative 0.04. Six columns, but only about two real ideas underneath.

PCA maximizes variance, so standardize first, or a big-scale column would dominate. Fitting PCA on the scaled data: the explained variance ratios are 0.485, 0.46, and then just 0.023, 0.016, 0.009, 0.007. The first two components alone explain 94.5 percent of all the variance — a steep cliff, then a flat tail.

You can also ask scikit-learn to choose for you by passing a target fraction — n_components equals 0.90 picks exactly 2 components, the smallest number that explains at least 90 percent of the variance.

Each row of components_ lists how much each original feature contributes. PC1 weighs equally on annual spend, basket size, and items bought — essentially a value axis. PC2 weighs equally on visits, app sessions, and email opens — essentially an engagement axis. PCA rediscovered the exact two hidden factors we built in.

Projecting down to those two components gives every customer described by just two numbers instead of six. Mapping back with inverse_transform and comparing to the original scaled data gives a mean squared reconstruction error of just 0.055 — very little was actually lost. Plotting the scree curve and the customers in PC1-PC2 space makes both patterns visible at once.

PCA is a rotation plus a discard. What you gain is fewer, uncorrelated features and a picture you can look at. What you lose is easy interpretation — PC2 is a blend, not a column your stakeholders recognize. Use it for visualization, taming correlated features, and as preprocessing before k-means on wide data — always fit it on training data only. To recap: PCA builds ordered, uncorrelated components capturing the most variance. Next, the Capstone: building your first models end to end.
